Exploratory analysis of raw dat¶

Load the two different data sets using pd.read_csv() and plot them using correct units and axis labels¶

  • sampling rate 40MHz
  • measurments in kV
In [5]:
sampling_rate = 40e6
signal_columns = ["P0", "P1", "P2"]

train_raw = pd.read_csv("DS19hn0_cm0_train.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 5))
for column in signal_columns:
    ax.plot(train_raw["time"] / sampling_rate, train_raw[column], label=column)

ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Voltage (kV)")
ax.set_title("Normal behaviour")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
In [6]:
test_raw = pd.read_csv("DS19hn0_cm0_test.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 5))
for column in signal_columns:
    ax.plot(test_raw["time"] / sampling_rate, test_raw[column], label=column)

ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Voltage (kV)")
ax.set_title("Partial discharge test data")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Are there any visual differences between the two data sets?¶

The normal data show relatively smooth, slowly varying three-phase signals with moderate noise and only occasional spikes. In contrast, the test data contain much larger and more frequent impulsive transients, especially at the beginning of the recording, indicating abnormal signal dynamics.

Characterize normal dynamics¶

Load DS19hn0_cm0_train.csv and divide the time series into episodes of 1000 samples¶

In [7]:
episode_size = 1000

def add_episode_id(data):
    n_samples = len(data) // episode_size * episode_size
    episodes = data.iloc[:n_samples].copy()
    episodes["episode_id"] = np.arange(n_samples) // episode_size
    return episodes

train_episodes = add_episode_id(train_raw)

from tsfresh import extract_features
from tsfresh.feature_extraction import EfficientFCParameters

    train_episodes,
    column_id="episode_id",
    column_sort="time",
    default_fc_parameters=feature_settings,
    n_jobs=1,
    chunksize=1,
    disable_progressbar=False,
)

Scale the time series features, using sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler¶

Tip: Combine tsfresh.transformers.PerColumnImputer and sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler into a pipeline to avoid the problem of missing numbers.

In [11]:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from tsfresh.transformers import PerColumnImputer

scaler = Pipeline(
    [
        ("imputer", PerColumnImputer()),
        ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
    ]
)

train_features_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(train_features)

Visualize your data set in the coordinate system given by the first and second principle component¶

In [15]:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(data=train_scores, x="PC1", y="PC2", s=35)
plt.title("Normal data in PCA space")
plt.show()

Describe the scatter plot (two sentences)¶

The normal episodes form a curved, ring-like distribution in the PC1-PC2 plane, with several dense local clusters rather than one compact cloud. A small number of points lie far from the main structure, indicating that the normal data still contain some variation between episodes.

Which features are dominating the first principal component?¶

After fitting sklearn's PCA transformer, the attribute .components_ is the modal matrix of the covariance matrix. Its columns are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and are called principal components.

In [16]:
pc1_loadings = pd.Series(
    pca.components_[0],
    index=train_features.columns,
    name="PC1 loading",
)

pc1_dominant_features = (
    pc1_loadings.abs()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
    .head(10)
    .to_frame()
    .assign(feature=lambda x: x.index)
    [["feature", "PC1 loading"]]
)

The first principal component is dominated by features extracted from the P2 signal. The strongest feature is P2__maximum (loading = 0.073419), followed by P2 linear-trend intercepts, upper quantiles (0.6 to 0.9), the sum of recurring values, and the total sum of values; therefore, PC1 mainly represents the positive amplitude and level of P2.

Visualize the test data set in the coordinate system given by the first and second principle component¶

In [22]:
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(data=test_scores, x="PC1", y="PC2", s=35)
plt.title("Test data in PCA space")
plt.show()

Compare the scatter plots of both data sets¶

The two data sets overlap in the central PCA region, indicating that some test episodes still have feature patterns similar to normal operation. However, the test data are shifted towards lower PC2 values and have a much wider spread along PC1, including several extreme points at high PC1 and low PC2 values. This broader and shifted distribution suggests that the test signal contains abnormal dynamics consistent with partial-discharge behaviour.

In [23]:
comparison_scores = pd.concat(
    [
        train_scores.assign(dataset="Normal"),
        test_scores.assign(dataset="Test"),
    ]
)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=comparison_scores,
    x="PC1",
    y="PC2",
    hue="dataset",
    s=35,
)
plt.title("Comparison of normal and test data")
plt.show()

Concept study for predictive maintenance¶

Are there any indications for a partial discharge? If yes, when did they happen?¶

Yes. The test data show strong impulsive transients that are not present to the same extent in the normal data, which is consistent with partial-discharge activity. These events are concentrated mainly within the first approximately 0.005 s of the recording, with particularly large excursions around 0.002-0.004 s; a few isolated transients also occur later.

In [24]:
test_episode_times = (
    test_episodes.groupby("episode_id", sort=False)["time"]
    .min()
    .div(sampling_rate)
    .reindex(test_scores.index)
    .to_frame(name="start_time_s")
)

Fit a DBSCAN model on the train data and find a suitable value for hyperparameter eps to identify the outliers¶

  • Visualise your solution
In [25]:
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

min_samples = 5

neighbors = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=min_samples)
neighbors.fit(train_scores)

distances, _ = neighbors.kneighbors(train_scores)
k_distances = np.sort(distances[:, -1])

plt.figure(figsize=(9, 5))
plt.plot(k_distances)
plt.xlabel("Sorted episode index")
plt.ylabel(f"Distance to {min_samples}th nearest neighbour")
plt.title("K-distance plot for DBSCAN")
plt.show()

eps = np.quantile(k_distances, 0.98)

train_dbscan = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=min_samples)
train_labels = train_dbscan.fit_predict(train_scores)

train_dbscan_results = train_scores.assign(cluster=train_labels)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(
    data=train_dbscan_results,
    x="PC1",
    y="PC2",
    hue="cluster",
    palette="tab10",
    s=35,
)
plt.title("DBSCAN on normal data")
plt.show()

test_labels = test_dbscan.fit_predict(test_scores)

test_dbscan_results = test_scores.assign(cluster=test_labels)
test_dbscan_results = test_dbscan_results.join(test_episode_times)
